mcqs.q: Each dentinal tubule contains the odontoblastic process, dentinal fluid and:
mcqs.explain: Dentinal tubules contain the odontoblastic process, dentinal fluid and afferent nerve terminals; the odontoblast cell bodies remain in the pulp.

mcqs.q: In a LONGITUDINAL ground section, the dentinal tubules appear as:
opts: Parallel lines following an S-shaped course
mcqs.explain: In longitudinal section the tubules run as parallel lines, showing the S-shaped primary curvature in the crown.

mcqs.q: In a TRANSVERSE (cross) section, dentinal tubules appear as:
opts: Open circles surrounded by peritubular dentin
mcqs.explain: In cross-section the tubules appear as open circles, each ringed by dense peritubular dentin, set within intertubular dentin.

mcqs.q: The dense ring of dentin immediately around each tubule is the:
mcqs.explain: Peritubular dentin forms the dense ring lining each tubule; intertubular dentin is the bulk between the tubules.

mcqs.q: The S-shaped course of dentinal tubules in the crown is called the:
mcqs.explain: The S-shaped pathway of the tubules through the crown dentin is the primary curvature; it flattens to a straighter line in the root.

mcqs.q: Compared with the crown, the dentinal tubules in the ROOT are:
opts: Flatter / more linear (the S-shape flattens out)
mcqs.explain: As you pass into the root, the S-shaped primary curvature flattens to a more linear shape.

mcqs.q: The minor spiral-like kinks along the primary curvature are the:
mcqs.explain: Secondary curvatures are minor spiral-like kinks/irregularities along the length of the primary (S-shaped) curvature.

mcqs.q: The fine incremental growth lines of dentin are the:
mcqs.explain: The incremental lines of von Ebner are the fine growth lines of dentin; the lines of Retzius/perikymata belong to enamel.

mcqs.q: Contour lines of Owen differ from von Ebner lines in that they:
opts: Are accentuated, reflecting a major metabolic disruption during odontogenesis
mcqs.explain: Contour lines of Owen are accentuated lines reflecting a major interruption in dentin deposition (metabolic disruption).

mcqs.q: Dead tracts on a slide appear as:
opts: Dark/black areas of empty dentinal tubules
mcqs.explain: Dead tracts are empty tubules that appear dark/black by transmitted light; secondary/reparative dentin often lies beneath them.

mcqs.q: Interglobular dentin is identified in the:
opts: Crown, just below the mantle dentin (tubules cross it without peritubular dentin)
mcqs.explain: Interglobular dentin (hypomineralized) is found in the crown just below the mantle dentin; tubules cross it without peritubular dentin.

opts: In the root dentin, adjacent to the cementum
mcqs.explain: Tomes' granular layer is a layer of dark granules in the root, lying parallel and adjacent to the cementum (looping terminal tubules).

mcqs.q: The odontoblast cell BODIES are located in the:
mcqs.explain: Odontoblast cell bodies reside at the periphery of the pulp; only their processes extend into the dentinal tubules.

mcqs.q: On a decalcified longitudinal section, you can best demonstrate the:
opts: Odontoblast processes within the tubules (organic part)
The pulp blood vessels in detail
mcqs.explain: A decalcified section shows the organic part — the odontoblast processes within the tubules and intertubular dentin.

mcqs.q: A 56-year-old with a deep carious tooth had NO pulp exposure during deep caries removal. This is because of:
mcqs.explain: With age, secondary (and reactive tertiary) dentin causes pulp recession, so a deep cavity is less likely to expose the pulp.

mcqs.q: Enamel spindles, sometimes seen near the DEJ, are:
opts: Odontoblast processes that have crossed into the enamel
mcqs.explain: Enamel spindles are odontoblast processes that have crossed the DEJ a short distance into the enamel.

mcqs.q: The bulk of dentin between the tubules is the:
mcqs.explain: Intertubular dentin (fine collagen + apatite) lies between the tubules and forms the main bulk of dentin.

saqs.q: Where are the odontoblast cell bodies and processes located?
saqs.a: Cell bodies in the pulp (periphery); processes (Tomes' fibres) in the dentinal tubules, along with dentinal fluid and afferent nerve terminals.

saqs.q: How do dentinal tubules appear in longitudinal vs transverse section?
saqs.a: Longitudinal: parallel lines with an S-shaped course; transverse: open circles ringed by peritubular dentin within intertubular dentin.

saqs.q: Describe the primary and secondary curvatures.
saqs.a: Primary curvature = the S-shaped course in the crown, flattening to linear in the root. Secondary curvatures = minor spiral kinks along the primary curvature.

saqs.q: Distinguish lines of von Ebner from contour lines of Owen.
saqs.a: Von Ebner = fine incremental growth lines. Owen = accentuated lines marking a major metabolic disruption during odontogenesis.

saqs.q: How are dead tracts identified on a slide?
saqs.a: As dark/black areas of empty dentinal tubules, often with secondary/reparative dentin beneath them.

saqs.q: Where are interglobular dentin and Tomes' granular layer found?
saqs.a: Interglobular dentin: in the crown, below mantle dentin (tubules cross without peritubular dentin). Tomes' granular layer: in the root, adjacent to cementum.

saqs.q: Why might a deep cavity in an older patient avoid pulp exposure?
saqs.a: Because secondary (and tertiary) dentin deposition causes pulp recession (smaller chamber/obliterated horns), so the pulp is set back from the cavity.
